forces: Trumpets, horns, oboes, bassoon, strings and continuo
performers: Marine Chamber Orchestra of the United States Marine Band; Major Michelle Rakers, conductor
question: What can change when twelve bars are played three times?
intro: The shortest dance of the suite has twelve bars: a four-bar strain and an eight-bar strain, each repeated. The edition tells the players to repeat the whole air three times over, and in this recording the third pass is noticeably louder.

sections.label: Third pass · louder
sections.mNote: same strains, about six decibels louder than before

cues.title: Twelve bars, three times
cues.text: A twelve-bar dance: a four-bar strain and an eight-bar strain, each repeated, so one pass lasts about 24 seconds. The edition prints “This Air to be played 3 times over”, and the recording plays it three times, the strains ending near 0:05, 0:09, 0:16 and 0:25.
cues.evidence: HHA p. 53 prints the twelve bars, the repeat signs and the instruction; IMSLP lists the movement as 12 bars (36 played three times). Brief dips to −22.6 dB at 4.78 s, −23.8 dB at 8.68–8.78 s, −24.5 dB at 16.53–16.65 s and −23.1 dB at 24.61–24.68 s mark the strains of the first pass; further dips at 24.6 s and 48.0 s divide the recording into three passes of 23.5, 23.4 and 24.8 s. Twenty-four bars in 23.5 s is 0.98 s a bar; the onset-tempo estimate is 123 beats a minute.

cues.title: A French dance among English ones
cues.text: The Marine programme says Handel took the English style in a “Purcellian hornpipe” and the French style in several French dances. The Bourrée is one of the French dances, written in cut time with a one-note upbeat.
cues.evidence: Programme note for the Marine Chamber Orchestra concert of 29 January 2017: https://web.archive.org/web/20251101025231id_/https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Programs/170129.pdf?ver=2017-01-24-094649-630 . The cut-time signature and the one-note upbeat are on HHA p. 53.

cues.title: Louder to the last chord
cues.text: Since 0:48 this pass has run about six decibels above the first two, with the same printed notes; the recording does not show how the extra weight is made. The repeated eight-bar strain begins near 1:04, and a 4–3 suspension in the figured bass leads to the last held chord.
cues.evidence: The relative level is −18.1 dB at 48.0 s, −10.1 dB at 48.5 s and −7.3 dB at 49.5 s; its mean is −15.1 dB for 2–48 s and −9.4 dB for 49–70 s. HHA bars 11–12: the bass figures 4–3, then a final dotted minim. The relative level falls below −22 dB at 72.98 s. The third pass runs from about 48.2 to 72.5 s, so its repeated eight-bar strain starts near 64.4 s.

transitions.title: Closing cadence, then the dance restarts
transitions.how: The eight-bar strain ends its repeat on a held D with a 4–3 suspension in the figured bass before it (bars 11–12), and the dance starts again from the upbeat with no link. The recording dips only briefly, to about −23 dB for under 0.1 seconds, so the three passes run on almost without a break. The instruction “This Air to be played 3 times over” makes the restart part of the written music.
transitions.evidence: The relative level dips to −23.1 dB at 24.61–24.68 s. HHA p. 53 (bars 11–12, figures 4–3, final dotted minim) and Arnold’s 1788 score, p. 50, where the strain ends.

transitions.title: The same cadence, a louder restart
transitions.how: The second pass ends as the first did, with a dip to −24 dB at 48.0–48.2 seconds. The third pass then starts about eight decibels louder than the end of the second and stays about six decibels above the first two passes. The printed notes are identical; the recording does not show whether more instruments join or all of them play louder.
transitions.evidence: The relative level is −18.1 dB at 48.0 s, −10.1 dB at 48.5 s and −7.3 dB at 49.5 s; mean −15.1 dB for 2–48 s and −9.4 dB for 49–70 s. HHA p. 53 prints one statement of the twelve bars for all three passes.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Marine Chamber Orchestra, United States Marine Band (orchestra), Major Michelle A. Rakers (conductor)
fields.note: Commons gives the conductor as Major Michelle Rakers; the programme prints Major Michelle A. Rakers. No roster of individual players is published in the consulted sources. The wide shot in this video’s thumbnail shows a harpsichord at stage left, strings with a double bass and a bassoon; a trumpet is visible in the Hornpipe video, and no frame shows horns or oboes. Which sections play in each of the three passes is not established: an independent look at the official video reports upper-string players resting at about 0:34, where the printed score gives them notes, so the recording is not assumed to follow the printed parts. No orchestra view is authored for this movement for that reason.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Performing edition not identified. The movement number (15 of the three suites) and the structure heard (a four-bar and an eight-bar strain, each repeated, the whole air played three times) match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text and its instruction “This Air to be played 3 times over”; no editor or continuo realisation is credited.
fields.note: The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The structure follows from the measured pauses and the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962), which prints 12 bars with repeat signs and the instruction on p. 53; IMSLP lists the movement as 12 bars played three times (36). The higher level of the third pass is a feature of this performance: the printed notes are the same for all three.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Commons gives performance_date 2017-01-29; the programme prints Sunday, January 29, 2017 at 2:00 P.M.; the official video description repeats the date. The Handel group stands after the intermission in the programme. The Commons composition_date field, 1717-07-17, is the date of the documented first performance on the Thames, not a composition date.

composer.epithet: A German-trained composer of Italian opera who made the English chorus an actor in public musical drama.
facts: With Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; theatre work in Hamburg; study and commissions in Italy, 1706–10
Hanover briefly; settled in London in 1712; became a British subject in 1727
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos, chamber cantatas and ceremonial orchestral music
composer.background:
Handel grew up in Halle, the son of a barber-surgeon, and studied with Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow, organist of the town’s principal church. Zachow’s teaching included counterpoint, keyboard playing and the copying of other composers’ music. Handel briefly enrolled at the university and held an organist’s post before moving to Hamburg in 1703. Its public opera house offered a different education: he played in the orchestra and encountered the practical demands of singers, stage machinery and mixed theatrical repertory. His first opera, Almira, was performed there in 1705, with a German text incorporating Italian arias.

From 1706 to 1710 Handel worked in Italy, writing cantatas, sacred music and opera for patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Rome gave him access to virtuoso singers and to instrumentalists associated with Corelli. The Latin Dixit Dominus of 1707 demands rapid, independent choral lines and sustained control of dissonance; the chamber cantatas make emotional turns within much smaller forces. Agrippina, performed in Venice at the end of 1709, assembles much previously written material into a calculated theatrical comedy. Reuse was already part of his method: a successful musical gesture could acquire a different function when assigned to a new character and situation.
